speechtext:
Of course, Mr. Speaker, the right hon. gentleman, being an old and experienced member of the house, knows perfectly well that his question is totally out of order because he is asking me to confirm or deny
a newspaper report, which our standing orders forbid us to do. But since the right hon. gentleman has given me a very welcome opportunity to say something about this subject, I am very happy to make a brief statement about it.
My statement is this. The policy of this government in this matter is well known. It was iterated and reiterated a dozen times by my predecessor at the last session of parliament, and it is a policy that was instituted by the right hon. gentleman's government, which he seems to have forgotten. It is that the railways were invited to indicate to the board of transport commissioners all the lines that they were even considering abandoning, on the understanding that no abandonments would take place and no hearings would be held until the new legislation had been disposed of.
That, we thought, was one of the good things done by the previous administration. We still think this is a good idea, and I am happy to say that was the position the railways agreed to take. I do not know that we could have imposed it on the railways, or at least on one of them, but they accepted it.
My hon. friend the President of the Privy Council gave notice in the last session of parliament of a resolution to precede a bill which was set out in detail in Votes and Proceedings, I think on December 6, and it is the intention of the government to recommend to parliament, if the house approves the appropriate resolution, a bill to set up a railway branch line rationalization authority which, if parliament also approves, would be under the jurisdiction of my hon. friend from Calgary South, the Minister of Agriculture, who naturally would have at heart the interests of the most important of all users of the railways, namely the wheat farmers.
It was not by accident that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister chose the Minister of Agriculture for this responsibility, because he felt that this would be a tangible way of indicating to the farmers of western Canada that the interests of the producers would be put first and the balance sheets of the railways, as I said the other day, would have to take second place in this matter.

When we were discussing this item at six o'clock yesterday I was in the process of making a few remarks on two aspects of the minister's statement. The first had to do with NATO, and I was asking the minister if he would, in the course of this discussion, tell the committee something about the proposal to create a NATO multilateral nuclear force. I think this committee and the people of Canada are entitled to know what proposals have been made in this regard and whether Canada has received any invitation to participate in such a force. I think too we should like some assurance from the government that Canada will not participate until this matter has been fully discussed in the House of Commons.

Supply-External Affairs
There are many Canadians who support NATO in its role of seeking to deter military aggression in Europe but who, nevertheless, would be strongly opposed to a multinational nuclear force being set up by that organization. I think it has been commonly known that for some years West Germany has been exceedingly anxious to become an independent nuclear power. There are many of us who feel that the setting up of a multinational nuclear force would simply be using the back door in order to accomplish this end, and I should certainly like to have some assurance from the minister that no such step will be taken by Canada and that if Canada is approached in this regard the matter will be thoroughly discussed in this house. We have already had some experience of the government entering into treaties for the acquisition of nuclear arms without referring those treaties to parliament. We certainly do not want to wake up one morning to find that a multinational nuclear force has been established, that Canada is a member of such a force, and that this house has had no voice in reaching that decision.
The second matter about which I was desirous of making some comment is the part Canada is playing in the peace keeping assignment on the island of Cyprus. I think we all recognize that this is a role which Canada is ideally fitted to play. We have neither the wealth nor the technological know-how to be a nuclear power, but we have a part to play; and the most effective role we can perform is that of contributing to peace keeping forces in various parts of the world under the direct control and direction of the United Nations.
While I agree with all that has been said about the inequity of Canada having to bear the entire cost, nevertheless I believe that whatever the expenditures we are making in this regard, they will be much more worth while than many of the expenditures we have made in the past for military hardware which became obsolete before it was produced. But as to the cost of these operations, I certainly think the cost of any peace keeping operation ought to be borne by all the nations which belong to the United Nations.
I think most Canadians are wholeheartedly in support of Canada making this kind of contribution to the peace of the world. However we should recognize two things; first, that in a delicate situation such as this the Secretary of State for External Affairs finds himself in a difficult position. He is dealing with the United Nations, and if the communications which are sent to him are secret and confidential he has to recognize that fact. I think we must also recognize that when we turn forces over to the United

Nations they come under United Nations command, and that to some extent we have lost our national sovereignty in that respect. On the other hand I think we, as members of parliament, ought to say to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that we hold him accountable and responsible for seeing to it that the troops which Canada contributes to United Nations peace keeping operations are fully protected and are given every opportunity to carry out effectively the task which has been assigned to them.
The second thing which has to be recognized is that the secretary general of the United Nations is in an equally difficult position. He has, in Cyprus particularly, a most delicate mission to perform. This is not an instance in which United Nations forces are dealing merely with aggression. In that case the operation, though it might be a serious one, would be comparatively simple; where an act of aggression has been committed the responsibility of the United Nations is to stop the aggressor and protect the victim nation. But in Cyprus we are dealing with a civil war, and a civil war which is all the more serious because it affects two neighbouring nations which gave every indication of their intention to intervene. Had they intervened they could easily have started a conflagration which might have spread throughout the Mediterranean and perhaps throughout the world.
In carrying out the instructions of the security council to send a peace keeping force to Cyprus the secretary general of the United Nations had, therefore, to have the consent and the authorization of the government of that country. In consequence I am sure that a certain amount of negotiation and compromise was found necessary.
But bearing this in mind, I am sure that we as members of parliament must make it clear both to the secretary general of the United Nations and to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who is our spokesman before that body, that there are three things about which we are concerned. We are concerned, first of all, that the Canadian troops who have become part of the United Nations peace keeping force shall have full and complete authority to protect themselves at all times and take whatever measures may be necessary to carry out effectively the task which has been assigned to them. They must never be allowed, because of red tape, to find themselves in a situation in which the directives they have been given are inadequate to provide complete protection. They must never find themselves in a position where those directives are so indefinite that

they do not give them the clearest possible mandate to do the job which they have been sent to Cyprus to do.
The second thing we have to make clear to the secretary general is that the Canadian forces must not be hampered in carrying out their duties; that once an agreement has been reached with the government of Cyprus the United Nations forces must have freedom of movement and access to whatever areas require their presence, and that they will not be hamstrung by interference or manipulation.
Third, I think we have to make it clear to the United Nations that in our opinion there must be an eventual disarming of the guerrilla forces on the island of Cyprus. As long as there are bands of armed civilians roaming about Cyprus there is almost certain to be trouble, and this is almost certain to involve the United Nations peace force. I know it has been suggested in press reports from Cyprus that the government of Cyprus would prefer that any disarming of civilians be left to the Cypriot government. Normally this would seem to be a logical conclusion. The fact remains, however, that it is doubtful whether the Turkish Cypriots would be as prepared to accept disarming by the Greek Cypriots as they would by the United Nations forces.
The situation is further complicated by the reports, which I presume are accurate, that the Cypriot government has already taken many of their armed civilians into the militia, and therefore they would not normally be disarmed. I think it is very easy to visualize what will happen. If the Greek Cypriots endeavour to disarm the Turkish Cypriots while the Greek Cypriots themselves continue to be armed, under the pretence that they are part of the militia, it seems to me that the whole armed conflict will erupt once again. I know this has to be negotiated and that it is not easy to reach these goals quickly, but I think it has to be said in this parliament and it has to be recognized by the secretary general of the United Nations that we would feel much easier in our minds if steps were taken promptly to begin the disarming of civilian guerrillas, both Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots, thereby lessening the likelihood of bloodshed and lessening the chance that the United Nations peace keeping forces, the Canadians amongst them, might be caught in a crossfire between these two groups.
Mr. Chairman, I think we in this parliament have to recognize that the human race is now in the process of building something which is entirely new in human history. We are seeking to build, brick by brick, a system of collective security based on the rule of law. There aren't any precedents; there are no established patterns, and we have nc
Supply-External Affairs techniques for carrying this out. Men have long dreamed of the idea of the rule of international law, but to build up the kind of forces required, to decide the chain of command, to agree on the methods that will be used has to be worked out painfully and painstakingly. Therefore I think we have to be extremely patient. We have to recognize that if we are to have collective security based on the rule of law, there must be some surrender of national sovereignty both by any nation where a peace keeping force is operating and by the nations which contribute forces to the international police force. For that reason one cannot take too hard and fast a position. We have to feel our way. We will have to take a pragmatic approach. It will have to be a process of trial and error.
I think we are fortunate in the secretary general of the United Nations, who is a very distinguished gentleman. We are fortunate in the mediator who has been selected to endeavour to bring together the various factions in Cyprus. But I think as members of this house it is our responsibility to remind the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the secretary general of the United Nations that we, having decided to send these men to Cyprus, feel we have a responsibility, and that we intend to discharge that responsibility and shall keep on insisting that the terms of reference, the directives and the status of forces agreement which is now being negotiated shall all take cognizance of the three points I have mentioned; namely, the complete right of self defence and full protection for our forces; free movement and the right to go wherever it is necessary to go to perform their duties, and that we urge upon the United Nations and upon the government of Cyprus the necessity for moving very quickly toward the disarming of the guerrilla bands as a first step toward bringing peace and harmony on the island of Cyprus.
I hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs will express these concerns to the secretary general of the United Nations, and that he will tell the officers of the United Nations that the members of parliament and the people of Canada are concerned and would like to know more about the terms of reference and the directives, because we hold those who sit in positions of responsibility accountable for the Canadians whose lives and well being we have placed at the disposal of the international police force.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to cover the ground already covered, but last evening I asked a number of questions of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and was far from satisfied with the
1704	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs answers I received. I again return to the question that was mentioned in a passing way by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, the leader of the New Democratic party. I refer to the circumstances under which Canadians will serve in the force in Cyprus.
I am not here for the purpose of endeavouring to secure information which ought not to be available to us, but I think when the Canadian people provide an armed force which constitutes a large part of the peace keeping force in Cyprus, and pay the shot as well, parliament has the right to the information which has not yet been vouchsafed to us.
I mention this because the position taken by the minister last evening was that the information for which I asked would cause great difficulty if it were given. Indeed, he said it would be a matter of serious concern. I know he was not too serious when he said that, although when one reads it in Hansard-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: REVIEW OF FORMULA TO DETERMINE DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext: I was very serious.

maintopic: REVIEW OF FORMULA TO DETERMINE DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
I will deal with the question of seriousness in a moment. These words are so far removed from the usual way the hon. member replies to questions that I am going to place them on Hansard again. He said, as reported at page 1678:
I am sure my hon. friend would not want the country to get the impression that they cannot defend themselves.
I am the one he was referring to as "my hon. friend".
I assure my hon. friend that the directives will enable them to defend themselves to the full. I must say to my right hon. friend, the former prime minister, that knowing the responsibilities of government and knowing the situation in Cyprus, what he said today was not calculated to assist in the discharge of that very difficult assignment.
That was simply a ridiculous coup monte and nothing else. The information I asked for is available in the press. Surely the minister would not have the committee believe that that which is available in the press should not be available to parliament. I have an article before me which appeared in a newspaper of yesterday's date, and I should like to quote from it. It has to do with an interview which the writer of the article had with Archbishop Makarios.
British officers and soldiers have complained bitterly that they have been powerless to keep the peace without the right to disarm civilians, to make arrests, order curfews, or remove roadblocks.
The United Nations force is operating under the same limitations-
I ask the minister whether it is not correct that these limitations have been imposed, that they are known to exist. I suggest to him that details respecting these limitations, about which fullest information has been given to the press, should be revealed to parliament. I


recognize there are matters of security which do limit the extent of the information which can be given, but I hope the hon. gentleman is not falling into a habit which has become all too common with ministers opposite, namely that of refusing to give facts to parliament or indeed of presenting facts in a way which does not reveal the true situation.
We in Canada are most desirous to do our part to ensure and maintain the peace of the world within the limitations which are incident to our population and position. We are going to spend several million dollars on this force. We are doing so when certain of the powerful nations of the world which are members of the United Nations are deliberately refusing to make contributions. I could point to the U.S.S.R., which is in default I believe some $59 million; France is in default some $40 million for the peace keeping operations; and other countries as well refuse to play their part even in assisting the financing of the peace keeping operations which are of the essence of an effective United Nations. That being so, surely Canada has the right to know the circumstances under which this force, part of it placed under United Nations command, is going to operate. I ask specifically and within those limitations of security which are necessary why it is that members of parliament have to secure information from the press rather than in parliament.
There is another matter which has recently arisen, within the last few days, concerning NATO. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam referred to this body. I am not as optimistic as I was about the future of NATO. There has been a weakening of that body and in its collective purposes during the last couple of years. That is understandable. So long as there is threat of armed conflict, those who are joined together in concert to meet a potential danger or threat tend to remain united. When the threat is lifted the cement, as it were, which holds the organization together becomes weakened. I believe in this institution. I do not think we would be here had it not been born some 15 years ago and stood effectively united against the overwhelming threat which has faced not only western Europe but all mankind.
However, those who believe that the threat is now gone belong to a school who have not carefully studied events since 1945. Every now and then there is a defrosting between east and west. Every now and then there have been hopes that new detentes have been established, but after a period of time the west is suddenly brought to the realization that the aims and purposes of communism are unchanged and that these detentes, if you can

call them that, have often simply been detours on the part of the U.S.S.R. That being so, we must maintain NATO.
Therefore I ask the minister why it is that he or his office has taken the unprecedented step in the last few days of cancelling the biennial tour of Canada by the young European NATO political leaders. I understand that the American segment of the tour will go on as scheduled but that the normal four days' stay in Canada of these young, potential political leaders has been withdrawn. The information I have is that it was at the suggestion of the Department of External Affairs. I have a great deal of information on the subject but I shall not read it into the record.
I know that when young Canadians went abroad in 1961 and 1962 they learned more about NATO than they could have learned in any other way, and they came back to Canada imbued with an appreciation of and an enthusiasm for the institution, and were able to carry this message to their respective colleges and universities. This group which was to come consists of some 25 youth leaders. Two years ago I met a group like this when they came to Canada. They formed a warm impression of Canadian friendship and, above all, they came to understand the determination of Canada to stand with NATO.
I hope it is not correct that these NATO country youth leaders are to be told Canada is not interested in them. Unless they are welcomed here that is the impression they will get. I have the correspondence that has passed between the Department of External Affairs and interested persons in Canada, and I trust the minister will have this matter looked into at once. Canada cannot afford to ostracize herself from the opportunity to have the representatives of 15 countries come here. We place ourselves in a most unenviable position unless whatever directions have been given in this connection are revoked. If they are not revoked it will mean these young people will come to North America and not be the guests of a country that did so much to build up NATO.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: REVIEW OF FORMULA TO DETERMINE DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
I did not want to take up the subject matter of last night's discussion, but the right hon. gentleman has dealt with it again today and perhaps I owe it to him to make a reference.
I appreciate the attitude he takes as to the desirability of the house being fully informed on information that might be given without
Supply-External Affairs prejudice to the operation of the United Nations peace keeping force in Cyprus.
As I said last night, the right hon. gentleman had considerable experience as prime minister during the operations of the United Nations peace keeping force in the Congo, and I may recall that in 1961 a question was put to him with regard to the tragic loss of life among the Ghanaian contingent participating in that force. Happily in that particular situation Canadians were not involved, but the tragic circumstances provoked a question as to the right of the Canadian troops to defend themselves.
There was no doubt that the troops from Canada, and others in the United Nations force, had a right to defend themselves in that situation to the fullest possible extent, as they have on Cyprus. But I was interested in the reply the right hon. gentleman gave on that occasion, which can be found at page 4539 of Hansard for Tuesday, May 9, 1961. I mention this not because I wish to be controversial but because I want to state the problem. I am sure this will be appreciated by the right hon. gentleman and other members of the committee. On that occasion he said:
Canadian military personnel in the Congo are assigned to the United Nations and are under the authority of the United Nations Congo command. It is the United Nations command which has direct responsibility for the safety of United Nations troops, as well as for their effectiveness in carrying out their tasks.
He continued:
On the question of self defence, United Nations troops in the Congo are still under basically the same orders as those issued by the first United Nations commander, General Von Horn. These orders provided, in general, that members of the United Nations forces are authorized to use their weapons in self defence and to maintain positions which are considered tactically essential to the United Nations operations. These orders have been reinforced and given more detailed interpretation by the current commander, General McEoin.
Then he went on:
In the light of the special difficulties and dangers faced by this non-combatant peace keeping United Nations operation, Canadian members of the force have been given specific instructions by their Canadian commanding officer, derived from instructions issued by the United Nations commander. In essence the orders to Canadian troops provide that they may use their weapons for defence in certain clearly defined circumstances. Resort to force is, of course, to be used only if normal discussion or negotiation has proved impossible or unavailing.
No one took exception to that statement. Indeed, the present Prime Minister commented, inter alia, as recorded at page 4540 of Hansard for that date:
It may not be easy to lay down, in the words of the Prime Minister, the clearly defined circumstances which would justify the use of defensive

Supply-External Affairs
weapons, but X am sure every effort will be made by the United Nations to make sure that in the attempt to do that, the safety and security of those concerned is the first consideration.
It occurred to me that this exchange offered a parallel to the situation which currently engages our attention. The language which I used yesterday about the right of self defence, and more particularly a few days ago on orders of the day, was admittedly in general terms but not any more general, and understandably so, than the language used by the right hon. gentleman in the difficult circumstances that confronted the United Nations peace keeping force in the Congo.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, we must keep before us three documents; first of all, the terms of reference of the force, the directives given by the United Nations to the force commander and by the force commander to those under his command in Cyprus; and then there is the status of forces agreement.
With regard to the directives, I must say that these are in their very nature private and cannot, for the reasons I stated yesterday and on other occasions when this matter was discussed, be made public. In every operation of the United Nations this has been the practice, no less so in the case of the Congo than for other peace keeping operations of the United Nations. I suppose those with much greater military experience than I have had would say that this is true in any military operation, whether it be fully military or, as in this case, partly military.
With regard to the terms of reference of the United Nations force, and so we will have a complete record of this whole aspect of the problem, I should like to set out the terms of reference as provided in the resolution passed by the security council on March 4. They are in the following general words:
Recommends that the function of the force should be, in the interests of preserving international peace and security, to use its best efforts to prevent a recurrence of fighting and, as necessary, to contribute to the maintenance and restoration of law and order and return to normal conditions.
At first glance those words may seem to be far too general to offer an adequate basis for the activities of the United Nations force. I have compared these terms of reference with the terms of reference in other such basic documents of the United Nations, and I find that the language, while differing in some particulars, is basically the same. These particular terms of reference were carefully chosen and will remain the source of authority for the directives which will be issued to the force from time to time.
These directives are not immutable in character. They may be changed, and as situations arise will undoubtedly be varied

by new directives. It is obvious that in the discharge of the function of the force these directives, if made public, would not assist the very purpose for which the force was established and sent to Cyprus. This is particularly so in this situation which, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam pointed out, involves a rivalry between two communities on the island and an interest on the part of two neighbouring states.
It will be seen that the terms of reference and functions of the force empower the force, first, to prevent a recurrence of fighting; second, to contribute as necessary to the maintenance and restoration of law and order; and third, to promote a return to normal conditions. These terms of reference are sufficiently broad to cover an infinite variety of situations and activities in which the force may become involved without unnecessarily tying the hands of the force and of the force commander as to how he is to discharge his heavy responsibilities. I believe that the United Nations command will be in a position to deal with almost any situation, and that the directives which will flow from the terms of reference will be sufficiently elastic to allow the Canadian and other forces both to protect themselves and to take effective peace keeping action.
Commenting on what the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said, there is no doubt that we have the right, and we have asserted that right to see to it that the Canadians as well as other members of the United Nations force are able to take measures to protect themselves fully. Those measures will be taken in a manner calculated not to add to the difficulty involved in the assignment which has been given them.
I may say to the house quite frankly that on a number of occasions when I discussed matters involved in this question with the secretary general, both in New York and in Geneva, I told him about the interrogations that had been made in the house. He understood perfectly the concern of members of this house, a concern which he himself shares, to make sure that the opportunity of self defence is provided and that, to use the language of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, the force is not hamstrung in the activities which it pursues. I communicated again last night with the secretary general to make sure there would be no misunderstanding. As a result he has issued an aide memoire which I believe has been circulated to all member states, certainly to those interested in this particular operation, in the following words:
The terms of reference of the peace keeping force in Cyprus are set forth in paragraph 5 of the resolution adopted by the security council on March 4, 1964. The secretary general has instructed

the commander of the force that the activities of the force which are exclusively under U.N. command are to be kept at all times within the framework of the security council terms of reference and no action not entirely consistent with them is ever to be undertaken.
In addition, the commander of the force does receive from the secretary general from time to time as a matter of course both general and detailed directions relating always to the terms of reference for his guidance in the discharge of his command. This being in accordance with usual practice in a military force has been the rule scrupulously followed with regard to all other U.N. peace keeping operations. Naturally those directives are entirely internal and cannot be made available for any public use.
In the interests of the successful discharge of the heavy responsibility which has been placed on the shoulders of the secretary general, I believe he had no alternative but to take the same position as was taken by his predecessors. It is the same rule which has obtained in respect of United Nations operations in Korea and in the Congo, and I am sure it will be applied in any future peace keeping operations.
The role of the United Nations in Cyprus is that of a policeman, just as it is in UNEF, just as it is in the Congo. Like any policeman, his function is public knowledge and the manner in which he discharges that function takes place in the full glare of publicity. His mere presence discourages lawbreaking, but where that in itself is not enough he may apply the minimum degree of force to discharge his responsibility. He is authorized, in addition, to defend himself as necessary.
All these things we take for granted as part of the police function in an ordered society; yet we do not insist on publication of the instructions that the policeman receives from his chief every day, nor would it be conducive to the fulfilment of his responsibilities if his every movement and intention were broadcast for the benefit of potential wrongdoers. These conditions are identical with those under which the peace keeping force in Cyprus must operate.
I recognize that I have a responsibility as Secretary of State for External Affairs. It is not an easy one but I accept it. My duty, within the limitations laid down by the United Nations, has been and will continue to be consistent with the assignment given to the United Nations peace keeping force. It is to see to it that the Canadian and other members of the United Nations peace keeping force are not prejudiced in any unjustified way.
Now, what I have said with regard to disclosure does not apply to the status of forces agreement. Yesterday I mentioned that there were consultations under way in New York between the foreign minister of Cyprus and the United Nations with regard to the status
Supply-External Affairs of forces agreement. I am happy to say that agreement was concluded late last night. While I am not in a position at the moment to table the status of forces agreement, I hope to be able to do so within a short period- just as soon as the full text has been made available.
With regard to the question raised yesterday by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam, the status of forces agreement establishes explicitly that the force and its members, together with its vehicles, vessels, aircraft and equipment, shall enjoy freedom of movement throughout Cyprus. The status of forces agreement is in the main, although I have not got it for tabling at the moment, somewhat similar to the status of forces agreement for the Congo. I may say that because of the Congo experience, it was possible for the secretary general and his colleagues to prepare an agreement more quickly in this particular instance than in the other to which I referred.

Yes; as I indicated yesterday, it does. This is implicit in one of the clauses. I think it is section 11 of the agreement.
With regard to the question about multinational forces which was put to me by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, I would remind him of the announcement of policy made in this house on June 7, 1963 when the Prime Minister said, as recorded at page 790 of Hansard:
-I can assure the house, although I do not need to, that Canada has no intention whatever of developing national nuclear forces or of manufacturing national nuclear weapons. While we will give this proposal consideration, as indeed we are bound and are anxious to give consideration to any proposal made to us by any of our NATO allies-and we do not exclude the United States from that group-I do not think that it will be likely that we would wish to add to our existing responsibilities and commitments by participating in this kind of multilateral nuclear force. But this is a matter which will be given the consideration it deserves.
This proposal is not a NATO proposal. It is a proposal in which, consistent with this declaration of policy, Canada is not now participating.
With regard to the question of disarming guerrillas, I noted what the hon. gentleman

Supply-External Affairs said. He will recall what I said in that context a tew days ago in this house. The position of the United Nations with regard to this question is part of the directives and general principles laid down by the secretary general and of the aide memoire to which I have already made reference.
In so far as the question concerning young NATO parliamentarians is concerned, I have not got the full answer but I hope, before we are through, that I may have it. Perhaps I could give it later.

maintopic: REVIEW OF FORMULA TO DETERMINE DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
It is not my intention to delay the passage of this item, but since I have been here all week and my Easter holidays are shot a few minutes more will not do any harm. The reason I would like to speak on this item is that last year I was a member of the Canadian delegation attending the NATO conference. I must say this was an educational experience and one which was very useful.
There are 15 nations that make up NATO. They include Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Norway, France, Germany, Greece, Iceland, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Portugal, Turkey, the United Kingdom and the United States. Strictly speaking, NATO is considered a military alliance, but to my surprise I find there were other aspects to this organization. When the delegates were assigned to the different committees I found that I had been assigned to the scientific and technical committee. This committee dealt mostly with matters pertaining to agriculture.
Amongst the subjects discussed were land reclamation and water pollution. I took advantage of the opportunity to speak about P.F.R.A. during the meetings of this committee to which I had been assigned, and referred to what had been done under it so far as our prairie regions were concerned. I also informed the committee that we had another plan, namely ARDA. There were two countries that were very much interested in this new program which was approved in 1961, and they were the United States and Turkey. These countries are faced with problems similar to the ones we have in Canada. It was therefore gratifying to find that these countries were very much interested in these programs. I suppose other Canadian delegates who were assigned to this committee, such as the hon. member for Lanark, had a similar experience.
Another matter in which I was greatly interested was the attempt to bring the tariffs of the NATO countries into line so these countries would enjoy better trading relationships. All in all, I must say that this was a very successful conference. While NATO may be considered a military alliance at the moment, nevertheless I think as time goes on more and more countries will realize that the


other aspects of this alliance are very important. But these are important too, so that the relationship among these NATO countries may be such as to bring about greater harmony in all phases of our life.

maintopic: REVIEW OF FORMULA TO DETERMINE DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
I must admit that I did not realize until recently that the question of NATO was to be opened up and discussed the way it has been on a supplementary estimate. However since other members have opened up the entire subject of NATO and the Secretary of State for External Affairs has made some comment on it I feel obliged, myself, to make some comments and ask for some information with regard to this organization, our responsibility towards it in Canada, and decisions which have been made on the authority of the minister.
My first question arises out of the promise made across Canada by the Prime Minister that, having fulfilled the commitment allegedly made by the previous government with regard to nuclear arms, the present government would consult with the NATO authorities and endeavour to negotiate itself out of any nuclear position. My question is therefore: What action has the government taken through the minister of external affairs to negotiate Canada out of a nuclear commitment within the NATO framework?
I should like to follow this up with another question-I presume the hon. gentleman is the only one who can answer it. It is my understanding that there has been a renegotiation of Canada's commitment to NATO with regard to four R.C.A.F. squadrons in France. Will the Secretary of State for External Affairs be kind enough to give us a clear and lucid explanation of these negotiations which, I believe, were conducted a few months ago, based on the isolationist policy of de Gaulle who takes the position of God Almighty unto himself and declares he intends to develop his own nuclear force, irrespective of what the rest of the world or the NATO countries might think. We were told in the defence committee in Paris last fall that in exactly six years France proposes to have three atomic submarines all equipped with atomic missiles and that four years thereafter her entire military force, air force, army and navy, will be completely nuclear equipped. Having this attitude in mind, on what basis has the minister negotiated a change in policy concerning our four squadrons in France as a result of which two of these squadrons are to be moved from France to Germany but two are to remain in France because de Gaulle refuses, in accordance with his policy, to bring his own air force in Germany back to France because they could

not be nuclear equipped? He keeps his air force in Germany where it can be nuclear equipped by the United States.
On what basis are we now to keep two of our squadrons in France where they cannot be equipped in any way. I should also like to ask, under this new arrangement whereby two squadrons go to Germany from France and two are held in France, who is paying, Canada or NATO? Why, in the case of our two squadrons which remain in France, has there been a change to a reconnaissance and conventional role when these planes were constructed during the lifetime of the previous administration to perform a role which was solely a nuclear role? These changes have, I understand, been made in the last four months as a result of negotiations with NATO regarding our air force in France.
Since we are getting into a detailed discussion on NATO, let the minister give us an answer to at least these two questions. I ask him again, how far has progress been made with the commitment to renegotiate Canada's nuclear role in NATO and, second, on what basis do we maintain two air squadrons in France, non-equipped, when de Gaulle says France will keep hers in Germany, although we are maintaining ours in France itself to no purpose?

maintopic: REVIEW OF FORMULA TO DETERMINE DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
I only want to ask several questions. One affects the problem raised by my hon. friend from Vancouver East in relation to our policy in NATO toward France. It would seem to me, and I am not an expert in external affairs, that there must be some change in the attitude taken with regard to France. The fact that Canada finally succumbed to United States influence with regard to the possession of atomic weapons must have had some effect on French opinion and I am curious to know what the attitude has been and what, if anything, can be done to improve the relationship between France and Canada.
In the second place, I am extremely interested in the situation which has developed in Cyprus. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has done exactly what he has always done, and as ministers of external affairs have done for a very long time. He has talked a lot of mumbo-jumbo which members of parliament do not understand, and which I am sure the country is not supposed to understand, either. The subject of external affairs has always been in a field apart. I am always surprised to find that in my party, as I suppose in other parties, everybody who wants to be somebody wants to be an expert in external affairs. I have no such ambitions but I believe the question of Cyprus is so important that the Canadian public should understand what is happening and be well aware
Supply-External Affairs of what is going on. The minister used a number of Latin words which I do not understand, and it is not surprising we do not know what our troops are going to do. I now ask the minister of external affairs to tell us, not as a minister in charge of a department but as acting prime minister, why the request which was made by a number of members to the government, that they be provided with free transportation to Cyprus during what was to have been the Easter holiday, was denied.
Most of us do not speak the language of the participants in the cold war on the island of Cyprus. Speaking neither the language of the Turks nor the language of the Greeks, we would probably only be able to converse with those connected with the old British regime and others who were able to speak our language. I and the other members interested in going to Cyprus were not wishing to go there as a delegation of the government. We were not going there as representatives of a NATO organization or in any other official capacity; we were only going in order to find out some of the answers which I am sure we are not going to learn in the House of Commons, although some of these answers must be available to every soldier in Cyprus today.
I think it would not have hurt one little bit, because the V.I.P. plane-and I have checked this-is going to Cyprus with space available for three or four members of parliament if they want to go. These members were not asking that their expenses be paid by the Canadian people; we were only asking for transportation to Cyprus. We are willing to go there without the usual amenities that are afforded visiting members of parliament. I think this government was scared to let us go because we would know the answers to some of the questions that have been asked in this house.
I am sure that if I spoke to some of the soldiers in Cyprus they would be able to tell me what they are supposed to do on that island. I would be very surprised if they could not tell me, because if this were the case they would be doing whatever they wanted to do and would not be under direct instruction. I am sure that no secrets would be revealed if I were able to talk to the troops. I would be very surprised if the members of the Canadian contingent, or those of the Irish and the other contingents were able to find out anything that is of a secret nature, because of our inability to converse in the languages of the island. I know the hon. member is going to say that most of them are French, and this is perfectly true.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member tell us the names of the members who asked to go to Cyprus this week?

Supply-External Affairs

maintopic: REVIEW OF FORMULA TO DETERMINE DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
Arnold Peters was one. I cannot speak for the others, but I know that others wanted to go in an unofficial capacity. I can only speak for myself, and I asked to go. The Congo seems very far removed from here, but Cyprus does not seem so far away. I personally would have liked to go there to see what the economic situation is-not so much in terms of the orders given to the troops because, while this is important, that is their business and I agree with the minister in this respect. He is probably well aware of these instructions, and we presume the instructions are fair and reasonable and will afford protection to our troops. If this is not the case, we will replace the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Certainly the leader of the official opposition, in view of his past experience in connection with such forces, would know something of the guarantees that would be given in the circumstances.
I confess that I did not know where the island of Cyprus was and I had to look it up on the map. I suppose when I went to public school and studied geography I knew where it was, but I have forgotten since then because I suppose I have not been particularly interested in it; I have never had reason to pay it too much attention. I believe that we in Canada will have to make a different type of contribution to Cyprus in the form of economic assistance and, probably, technological assistance, before these problems can be settled.
I am told that most nations which have been concerned with the island of Cyprus have found things on that island to be too expensive, and one of the problems is that the amount of money that can be raised through the economy of that country is not sufficient to keep the people on the island. If this is so, members of parliament would be in a much better position to devise methods of helping the island if they visited that country. So what, if some members of parliament occasionally went to the army barracks and had a meal? I do not think this would bankrupt the government.
I think this club connected with the Department of External Affairs should not exist. I am of the opinion that this club has been very exclusive up to now and will have to be less exclusive in order that some members who are interested in this particular field may obtain some information.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: REVIEW OF FORMULA TO DETERMINE DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, before the hon. member attacks the club too strongly, may I just tell him that I know of no objection or law which would prevent my hon. friend going to Cyprus.

maintopic: REVIEW OF FORMULA TO DETERMINE DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not feel so strongly about it that I intend to pay for a commercial passage in order to go to Cyprus.

maintopic: REVIEW OF FORMULA TO DETERMINE DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: REVIEW OF FORMULA TO DETERMINE DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
I do not want to do this for a vacation. Four or five days in Cyprus would, in my opinion, not necessarily be a vacation at this time. Many people would find that out. I do not want to go there for social reasons. I wish to go there in order to ascertain some of the conditions that exist on the island and methods in which we can assist these people. I would be doing this in my parliamentary role.
I know the minister has not refused permission. Permission hinges upon whether transportation is given through another department. But I do think that if we are going to look intelligently at the problem as it affects Cyprus we will have to think, not so much in terms of roadblocks, of guerrilla bands in a particular area of the island, but in terms of the economic situation of the island community and the type of aid Canada could give to assist in the development of the island and its economy. We should also be giving consideration to what can be done to enable the two groups on the island to get along in harmony. It is my understanding that the poverty on that island is very severe and this is one of the deciding factors behind the operation of the guerrilla forces in the community. I have only read this.
If I had the opportunity to go to Cyprus, and if-there are many "ifs" in this-we had been given an Easter recess, and if I had been able to learn anything on arriving there in view of the fact that there would be a language barrier, I think I could have made a much greater contribution. I suggest to the minister that he should not be so reluctant in this regard. I think only a limited number of members would be willing to sacrifice four or five days in order to go to the island. It seems to me that if we went in a non-official capacity-and certainly we would have to go in such a capacity, or we would be a delegation-and were able to consider the situation in Cyprus and also in some of the other areas in which Canadian forces are involved, our understanding of these questions might be much greater than it is at the present time.
Yesterday the minister mentioned Yemen. I think I would not be too wrong if I said that most members of parliament do not know where Yemen is and have no idea of the conditions or people in Yemen. I may be wrong and I may be doing a disservice to members of parliament. But we are supplying to Yemen a certain number of Canadian personnel to help solve the problems of that country. According to some of the reports that

have been given us by the minister, this is a rather dangerous mission and there may be other things that are necessary in Yemen. Far be it from me to run myself down. I have met people from Yemen at the United Nations. I have heard some of the discussions, and I think we are perhaps overstating the situation. However I do think an opportunity should be given for members of parliament to visit these areas, provided such visits do not interfere with other commitments.
I agree that it would be different if this were to be a delegation. I think the Minister of National Defence will have to make the decision as to whether facilities are available for such visits. This is the responsibility of the people concerned, but I think there should be no reluctance to make allowances for these purposes. One of my friends keeps travelling around this part of the world. He was in several South American countries, and several times during his visits there happened to be a revolution in progress. I suggest that this is purely accidental, because he immediately leaves and the revolution goes on anyway. Many hon. members know the former member to whom I am referring, and it does seem unfortunate.
However, I do not think this will happen again and that the situation will be hurt by members of parliament.
I am sure the minister of external affairs, with his wide experience of travel across the world, will be of the opinion that greater understanding of the problems of the people to whom he speaks, including those in Cyprus, is essential, and this is made possible by his ability to visit these areas. I suggest the government reconsider the request which has been made by a number of members of parliament who would like to spend a few days in areas where Canadians are contributing to world peace. I think they should be allowed to make such a trip, not only with the encouragement of the government but also with the blessing of the minister of external affairs.

On the other hand, if we consider the amounts that are earmarked for foreign aid, we find that they represent about $2,250,000. With regard to the recognition of a government we would want to bear in mind the durability of tenure of the government itself. If this were apparent, all other things being considered equal we would extend de facto recognition. The question of de jure recognition would follow.
Recently we recognized a country with which we do not have any ideological community of interests. It had been admitted into the United Nations and as we were members of that body-I refer, of course, to Mongolia-we accorded that country recognition, although we do not presently intend to establish a mission there. Conditions there were similar to the situation that attended our recognition of Mongolia.
In the case of commonwealth countries the question of recognition does not usually arise. My right hon. friend will remember interrogating me one day with regard to the government of Zanzibar. In that instance we did withhold recognition because we wished to examine developments there, in consultation with other members of the commonwealth.
With regard to recognition generally, the situation would be much as I have stated. There are, of course, some countries with which we do not exchange diplomatic missions; this is one way of effecting recognition. The mere acknowledgement of the existence officially of a country is another way of extending recognition. In some countries the ideological complexion has had something to do with the policy of recognition, although we feel generally that the isolation of countries in this interdependent period in the history of the world is undesirable.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DISPOSITION OF GRADE EXCESS AND OVERAGE
speechtext:
I have two statements to make in connection with this bill. First, I have a few not too brief remarks on a matter of interest which was raised by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) as to the procedure which the Chair has followed in the past and is following at the present time with regard to assisting members, or whether or not members should receive notice that their bills are in order or not. I think it would be useful, generally speaking, if I made a statement with regard to the question raised by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi and then dealt with the bill which the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp) wishes to bring forward this afternoon.
The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi rose toward the end of February to direct a question to the Chair. The question is found in the following words on page 281 of Hansard of February 27:
Last session and the session before, a number of these bills were determined to be out of order at the time of second reading. I remember at one point speaking to the Chair about this, and the house leader for the government during the last session said he felt some method should be devised whereby private members could be informed before second reading if there were anything substantially wrong with their bills. I should like to ask the Chair whether any method has been worked out whereby private members might be given this information before second reading, and I do so in view of this caveat that has been entered to all these bills.
To summarize, the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi suggests that a member having a public bill before the house should be notified in advance, that is, before second reading, if the said bill is to be declared out of order. This cannot be done for different reasons. First, so many public bills have been introduced by private members that the study thereof may be completed, in some cases, only on the eve of their being called for second reading. Second, if the Speaker has any doubt as to a bill being in order it is possible, as often happens, that he might call on the members to assist him in coming to a decision. How could he do so if he had already advised the mover that his bill will not be accepted? To quote from Beauchesne, citation 71(6), page 61 of the fourth edition:
In all matters of doubt, the Speaker will consider attentively the opinions of members of experience, or sometimes, instead of expressing his opinion on either side, may ask instructions from

the house or reserve his decision on the point in discussion, or suggest that the house may, if it thinks proper, dispense with the rule in a particular case. In doubtful cases, he will be largely guided by circumstances.
In the third place, the Speaker has no assurance that all bills will be proceded with. Why, then, should he rule on bills which may never be called? The time to give a ruling is when a question is raised in the house. It certainly is not one of the duties of the Speaker to rule in advance on hypothetical questions or on points of law before they arise.
Citation 70(6) at page 60 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, is to the effect that-
The Speaker decides questions of order only when they actually arise and not in anticipation.
Now, citation 364 at page 270 states:
Leave to introduce a bill is not always granted as a matter of course. The house is free to refuse it-
In the citations which follow many examples are given where the Speaker rules out the motion for first reading as being out of order on the grounds that it involved a charge upon the revenue, or for other reasons. Evidently in those cases no previous notice could be given to the hon. members sponsoring such measures.
In the circumstances now prevailing, the members have the advantage that all their bills are introduced, receive first reading and are circulated. They have been given notice by way of a caveat that these bills will be studied and, if necessary to declare any out of order, that this will be done only after serious consideration. This procedure has been agreed to by the house itself.
May I remind all hon. members of a certain standing order which is to be found in our standing orders, and suggest that if any of them wish assistance in the drafting of public bills, or as to their legality, they should consult with the parliamentary counsel. It is up to the members to inform themselves as to the rules of the house and their application in the past. The guiding principle is declared in section 54 of the British North America Act and in our standing order 61. In other words, bills involving an expenditure of public money or taxation, and all measures involving a charge upon the people, must be preceded by a resolution. It should be noted also that a resolution is required not only when an amendment seeks to increase the amount previously approved by parliament, but also if it changes the modality and conditions of the grant authorized by the original legislation.
Therefore, before introducing their bills in the house, hon. members should take the trouble of reading the decisions of speakers
Disposition of Grade Grain in the past as found in Beauchesne's third edition, these decisions being summarized as comments following the related standing orders in the fourth edition.
The Speaker is the servant of the house and is responsible for the enforcement of its rules. As stated by Beauchesne:
He declines to submit motions to the house which obviously infringe the rules which govern its proceedings.
In other words, the Speaker does not make the rules but he is bound by them and by the decisions of former Speakers as they have been interpreted in the past.
So much by way of reply to the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi. I hope that statement will be of use to hon. members generally. I come, now, to the bill which is presently before the house, Bill No. C-17.
For different reasons, which I will try to summarize as briefly as possible, I must regretfully rule the motion for second reading of this bill to be out of order.
The argument made by the hon. member to justify the passage of this measure is found at great length in the preamble thereto, to which I will refer later on, and in the explanatory notes.
The preamble, for instance, states in its conclusion that "His Excellency the Governor General did not recommend the appropriation of grade excess and overage of the proceeds thereof to the use and purposes of the governor in council, as required under section 54 of the British North America Act" and also that "the amendments purporting to be so enacted are and ever have been unlawful of purpose and null and void in effect". In an attempt to further clarify the situation, it is stated in the explanatory notes to the bill that "Without the Governor General's recommendation, the 1955 provisions were and are unlawful."
Then the bill goes on to say that the full amount of the loss shall be paid out of the public officers guarantee fund or, if not, then recovered from the officials responsible and be disposed of for the construction of a public terminal elevator at the town of Tisdale and for other purposes. I am unable to see how such a plan could be worked out, nor am I ready to admit to the insufficiency of the resolution which preceded the introduction of "An act to amend the Canada Grain Act" in 1955. If there was a defect in the procedure there is no doubt that the point should have been raised and decided at that time. This has always been the position adopted by my predecessors and has been accepted by the courts.
For instance, as far back as 1926, in the exchequer court in the case of the King, plaintiff, and Irwin, defendant, where the

Disposition of Grade Grain defence had claimed that the Naturalization Act "was in the nature of a money bill and was not properly introduced into the house and was void" it was held, "that when a statute appears on its face to have been duly passed by a competent legislature, the courts must assume that all things have been rightly done in respect of its passage, and cannot entertain any argument that there is a defect of parliamentary procedure lying behind the act."
The argument for the validity of this act rests on premises which I unfortunately am unable to accept. To quote the words of Lord Halsbury in a decision respecting the commissioners for income tax, we must "proceed upon the assumption that the legislature is an ideal person that does not make mistakes."
And now Willis J. in Lee v. Bude and Tor-rington Junction Railway Co. (1871) L.R.6, C.P.576 at p. 582, used words which I would like to adopt. He said, "If an act of parliament has been obtained improperly, it is for the legislature to correct it; but so long as it exists as law, the courts are bound to obey it.. . Having neglected to take the proper steps at the proper time to prevent the act from passing into a law, it is too late now to raise any objections to it."
I therefore consider myself bound by the opinions and decisions I have referred to or cited, and cannot entertain any argument that there is a defect of parliamentary procedure lying behind an act as a matter of fact. It is, as has been said, a case where the maxim omnia praesumuntur rite esse acta applies with great force and rigour.
As the trust moneys mentioned in the bill and proposed to be recovered as suggested in clause 2 thereof for the general advantage of the beneficiaries cannot, by virtue of what I have already said, be so recovered, it seems Useless to repeat the reasons I gave last session in ruling out of order another bill of the hon. member respecting the Tisdale grain terminal on June 13, 1963, and which is to be found at pages 987 and 988 of Hansard of that date, or the ruling by Mr. Deputy Speaker on December 10 when he ruled out a government bill which had been introduced without a resolution. This was quite a lengthy decision so I will quote only a couple of lines. He said, "The new act will change the conditions attached to the spending of these moneys by the original act and, to this extent, the bill now before the house would appear to be a money bill."
Before closing my remarks I would refer to the drafting of this bill; more particularly to the long preamble of two pages and a

half, which is more in the nature of an argument, an explanatory note and a discussion, than in the proper and usual form of such part of a bill.
Standing order 72 provides expressly that, "No bill may be introduced either in blank or in an imperfect shape." In the caveat I gave on Thursday, February 20 on the introduction of 68 public bills by private members, I stated that each of these bills would be scrutinized and that if any defects were found therein so far as the practices and usages of the house are concerned, it would be brought to hon. members' atttention. This I am doing now. As stated by the conference of commissioners on uniformity of legislation in Canada in 1942, "Preambles should be avoided. An act should explain itself and if reference to a preamble is necessary in construing any provisions of an act, it would indicate that the draft requires revision."
Sir Allison Russell, K.C., expresses the same opinion in his book on legislative drafting when he further states, "It is only in exceptional cases, usually those where constitutional changes are being enacted, that a preamble is now used to explain the object of an act. A preamble cannot restrict or extend the enacting part, when the language and scope of the act are not open to doubt."
However, it is not mainly on account of the preamble that I have to declare this bill out of order, but for the reasons given previously.

I have been advocating this 12-mile limit for a great many years. I have done so because the

livelihood of 90 per cent of my constituents depends upon its being established, and I can assure the hon. member that my constituents are just as vitally interested in this matter as are the trailers of B.C.
However we must take a responsible attitude and realize there are such things as historic rights and treaties between Canada and other countries which cannot be treated as scraps of paper or brushed aside. Fishing has been the main industry in my province for over 400 years. It was carried on by the fishermen of European nations long before Newfoundland came under British rule and long before it was peopled with permanent settlers. Those nations acquired historic rights, and if we want to create a responsible image of Canada we must recognize these facts.
There is, however, another consideration, and a paramount one, the right of people to make a living. No civilized nation in the world could insist on retaining historic rights which result in depriving the people of a country of their means of livelihood. That is why I said at the outset that this bill was important to my province, and in particular to my constituency.
Each year, at about this time of year, the fish come in from the ocean and are very plentiful in a narrow strip of water along the west part of my riding, and it often happens that at this time of year the ice comes out of the gulf and encloses a sheet of water along the coast. In many places the ice comes in right to the land and at other places it stretches two or three miles off shore. Yet in that narrow strip of water, which is perhaps 80 miles long, not more than 12 miles wide at the widest point and diminishes in width almost to zero, 50 to 60 draggers belong to other countries fish. There are Spanish draggers, Portuguese draggers, French draggers, draggers from almost every European country one could mention. This is the time of the year when the fishery in this section of my riding is at its peak. My constituents are depending upon the fishery for their livelihood because either they get the fish now while they are there, or they do not get them at all. Their whole livelihood is at stake.
Yet with such a concentration of foreign draggers in this small stretch of water my constituents dare not go out to try to earn their livelihood. They cannot risk putting out their gear because these foreign draggers would destroy it. The gear costs thousands of dollars and many of my constituents have had their gear destroyed by the operations of these draggers. In this 12-mile wide stretch of water operations by foreign draggers can be
Coastal Fisheries Protection Act carried on with perfect legality and yet they result in taking away the livelihood of 7,000 or 8,000 people.

We have discussed this matter on many occasions in the past, but there has been some hesitancy in calling the committee together. I expect that in the very near future Canada will declare the 12-mile limit. It seems to me that one could go on at great length about the merits of the 12-mile limit. I have heard no suggestion from any quarter as to the disadvantages of it, particularly so far as our fishermen are concerned. There are two things that are being said from time to time in discussion of this problem in Newfoundland. The first is that it will be a difficult thing to enforce a 12-mile limit, hence there will not be the substantial improvement it is hoped there will be. It is said that trawlers or drag-gers will continue to violate, perhaps with greater ease, a 12-mile limit.
In so far as that is concerned, I would say the 12-mile limit would be easier to enforce than the 3-mile limit. In many areas, particularly along the eastern coast of Newfoundland, the fishermen actually go from six

If a trawler violates the 12-mile limit there will be a couple of miles of grace to apprehend the culprit. It would seem the 12-mile limit would leave a little leeway and would clear the ground for the inshore fishermen.
The inshore fisherman of Newfoundland is one who, in the past, has been lost in the shuffle. Perhaps I could cite a reason that the fishermen were not well disposed to confederation in 1949. In 1890 the Bond-Blaine treaty, which would mean so much to Newfoundland, was virtually scuttled by an unimaginative dominion government. I am very glad, and the people of Newfoundland are very glad to know that the present Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) and the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) are prepared to make atonement for this previous unimaginative and unenlightened action on the part of the Canadian government.
