Some time ago the question was asked, what is to be done under the Immigration Act in relation to the admission of nationals from countries to which various forms of restriction are applied?
The last time this matter was being discussed I mentioned that many of the Chinese immigrants who do enter this country enter under the authority of orders in council. The number involved is close to 40,000 people, every one of whom was an exception to the rules established by the act. I am informed that since then a large percentage of those who were permitted to live here by order in council have applied for the protection of the amnesties which were granted on at least three occasions by ministers in charge of immigration and citizenship.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration The difficulty which arises now is that the offences which took place prior to the last amnesty are continuing to take place. People are still entering this country illegally and applying under the order of July, 1962, for an amnesty in respect of their offence. This situation is serious because it comes extremely difficult to change or improve the immigration laws at a time when it is not possible to stop the lawlessness which is taking place under the existing provisions. The swing of the pendulum must be stopped before the act can be changed and modified.
What bothers me is that I have been made aware in various ways of a number of these cases, and I find that in each one little has been done to ascertain why the offence was committed in the first place. Some of these cases are unusual. One which came to my attention involves a father-a Canadian citizen-who sent his own daughter, also a Canadian citizen, back to China. She married her brother there and then brought him out to Canada as her husband. She has applied for regularization of the position under the terms of the amnesty, and this matter has now been resolved. Other cases are not so easily resolved. Some are still under investigation by the R.C.M.P., but when the inspection reached the stage of looking into the orders in council, that was the end of the matter.
In a legislative sense we have been able, by passing orders in council, to legalize what is essentially an illegal situation. This makes it difficult, if not impossible, for the R.C.M.P. to do anything about it. I had some dealings with several R.C.M.P. officers who were carrying out investigations in my riding. They of course were shortly told that they were not to visit me in the parliament buildings-that they were not to visit me at all. In fact this matter was closed.
I put a motion on the order paper for the production of all the papers and for the names of all the people involved. The reply was a voluminous one. I do not see how it will be possible for any individual to investigate these cases; I do not know how he would go about it. But I can say I am pretty disgusted with the R.C.M.P. and with the department itself for not pursuing these matters.
The nationals in this country who are vitally interested in the immigration laws were promised from time to time during the term of office of the former government that changes would be made. I give credit to the former government for stopping the orders in council; they stopped these exceptions to the law. This of course brought the whole process to a standstill in certain areas. Now I presume, we are going back to the old system of passing orders in council. I think it is a shame that we in this country cannot

find out exactly what has been happening in the past and see that it does not happen again.
I would like to suggest that the present minister is having a look at the channels of immigration in Hong Kong at the present time with a view to establishing the old system of bringing in immigrants under orders in council, so that he would have the opportunity of carrying out investigations which are outside the scope of the immigration branch. But I know that if we are really to be honest about what has happened in the past we must admit that there is hardly a member of parliament in this house who is not in the disgraceful position of knowing something about this immigration business, particularly about what has happened in the past with regard to Chinese immigration.
I do not think there is a member here who does not have some knowledge, and who is not now sitting tight and doing nothing about the knowledge he has.
I think this question must be brought out into the open so that everyone may know what is wrong with our immigration system, particularly as it affects Asiatics. If this frankness is expressed, the minister of immigration has an obligation to introduce new laws which will eliminate the excuse for abuses such as have taken place in the past. I have told the Chinese people in my riding that the government intends to change the immigration laws as far as the Asiatic people are concerned. I have told them that the government has promised to do this, that we have the word of the minister that it would be done this session. I cannot say that today, because hon. gentlemen opposite have not said they are going to change the law this session. But for three of four years we have been told that changes would be made. We have been given assurances to that effect. One investigating officer asked me how there could be these changes when the problems facing the immigration branch are the same now as they were four or five years ago, before the big investigation took place.
At the time the cabinet changes were made I was very hopeful that the then minister of citizenship and immigration would be left in charge of that department because he had done some good work with respect to the problems of Indian affairs. I had hoped he would be in a position to make certain decisions which would have clarified this situation with regard to immigration in general and Asiatic immigration in particular. Perhaps this only happens in my area, but I think if hon. members would really get around and talk to the Chinese people in their ridings they would find that many things are happening that have not been made public in the past. These are

the things, in the main, which we should prevent by legislating changes in the act. You cannot really blame a person in this country for wanting to bring over some of his close relatives, a son who is over the age of 21 or a mother who is under the age of 60, but very often these relatives do not meet the terms of the regulations as they apply at the present time. These people must wonder why we in parliament cannot solve some of the problems and why we allow the discrimination, that is so evident, to continue under the Immigration Act.
I see that the Minister of Justice is here. I think that perhaps he has more to do at the moment than he can handle. But if he has any time left over, I would like him to offer some assistance in the field of immigration because I know he has some understanding of the problem. This is a field that must be understood and a great deal of sympathy and consideration must be given to it. We in this country should be progressive enough to double our population in the next ten years. If we really wanted to do something for confederation we would increase the flow of immigrants into this country. We are a very large country in which many, many areas are not being developed at the moment because we do not have the population with which to develop them. I know the charge is often made that if we change the immigration laws and increase the number of immigrants into Canada we will increase unemployment. But in what fields would we increase unemployment? Is it not true that we will have to feed these people, house them, clothe them and provide the other services which are now surplus to our requirements? In this way we will be performing a great service to many of these countries which today are not able to feed and clothe their people.
I should like to know, Mr. Chairman, whether it is ^ the intention of the government to do nothing to solve the mess that is well known to exist in respect to immigration.
The other day I phoned an R.C.M.P. inspector because I was advised a particular matter came within his department. This matter concerned an investigation by the passport department of the R.C.M.P. The inspector said he would look into the matter and would phone back. This was several weeks ago. He has no intention of phoning back. Unless the government make up their minds that they want to do something about it, I am sure the inspector will not do anything about it, any more than will the constables further down the line. I thinV this is a field in which the government is very vulnerable, and we as a nation are
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration very vulnerable, because of the anomalies which exist in our Immigration Act.
I do not know whether the present minister intends doing anything about it, but I make the suggestion to you, Mr. Chairman, that he probably will not, because this is a department that requires a very strong minister. This problem requires someone who will spend a great many hours each day formulating a program that will cope with the problems which have obviously existed in the past. This situation requires someone farsighted enough to know that part of the future of Canada will rest upon the type of immigration policy that we develop.

I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to make a general comment about the Indian affairs branch, its structure and organization. For a period of 10 years one Colonel Jones was the director of the Indian affairs branch. Without attempting to say anything disrespectful about Colonel Jones as an individual, I am quite sure that the procedures and disciplinary concepts and attitudes of a colonel were taken holus-bolus from his military background and transplanted into the Indian affairs branch. Unfortunately, as a consequence I think the Indian affairs branch became somewhat ossified and fairly strict in whatever it attempted to do.
Let me cite an example. A couple of years ago the Indian affairs branch developed a policy with respect to Indian housing, in which there were four different methods that Indian people could participate in the building of houses. I phoned someone in the department to ask for a copy of the brochure outlining this scheme. It has been distributed far and wide among the agencies and the bands, but even though the person I spoke to on the phone said he would send me a copy, a week went by before I received it.
Normally when one is dealing with a government department and phones for something, somebody in the clerical section will put it in the mail, but in every request I made to the Indian affairs branch during the time Colonel Jones was there, there was always a delay. In this particular instance I got a letter from Colonel Jones about a week or so later, referring to the conversation I had with somebody else, and enclosing a copy
1728	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration of the brochure. I cite this as an example of the overly strict rigidity which prevented that department from doing anything worth while, other than in an administrative way, when Colonel Jones was the director.
Colonel Jones has now retired and the present director is Mr. Battle, who I gather is a person of an entirely different nature, background and interest, and many people in the branch hope, as I do, that Mr. Battle, with all the assistance he can get from the minister, will be able to transform the Indian affairs branch into something worth while. He has only been a short time in this position and miracles do not work overnight, especially when one tries to apply them to a branch such as Indian affairs.
When the main estimates for this fiscal year come before us, I hope the minister will be able to report on the changes that have been wrought in the Indian affairs branch and that we shall not have to persist in looking at it in a critical way, as has been necessary in the past.

I wish to read the words outlining this estimate. They are:
Welfare-operation and maintenance including grants and contributions as detailed in the estimates, $25,000.
And the detail shows:
Grant to the province of Manitoba towards community development.
This may be a play on words but I think it represents the psychological attitude of the people who prepare the estimates, an attitude which many people have adopted in regard to welfare, but I do not think a grant, or an expenditure of money made directly by the Indian affairs branch for the purposes of community development should be classified as "welfare", because is is not welfare. The sooner we get away from the concept of welfare as applied in the Indian affairs branch to our native people the better, especially as it is applied to keeping those people in almost abject poverty and starvation. I merely make this as a suggestion for the future, because such words and designations used by the people who prepare the estimates are not in keeping with the enlightened and forward approach which we should have to Indian affairs and the Indian people in this day and age.

I think the public are entitled to know what is the present state of the project called Ookpik, or something like that where a little imaginary owl developed in the Arctic has been violently abused, according to recent newspaper reports.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The suggestion is made that the point now raised by the hon. member does not relate to vote 70e.
Well, it very likely relates to the handicraft development program, though it may be the wrong department.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It relates to the Eskimos, not the Indians. The Indian affairs branch comes under the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, and that is what is before the committee at the moment. The Eskimos come under the jurisdiction of the department of northern affairs, and Ookpik belongs to the Eskimos.

That is downright discrimination in the handicraft field. It is disgusting when you go into many shops and see totem poles for sale that are manufactured in Japan. Not long ago I spoke to one Indian chap who was developing and selling native Indian handicrafts in Ontario and Quebec, and it was his opinion that the department was doing absolutely nothing to help in this field. He had made application for assistance here in Ottawa, and he had a small store. I would like to know why he found it so difficult to get assistance. He said many of the people he had contacted in the department were patronizing in their attitude, patting him on the shoulder and saying, "You are doing a fine job," but they were not really interested in helping him obtain genuine Indian handicrafts. He showed a great deal of initiative but I understand he has gone out of business since that time.
In the northern areas especially there seems to be no co-operation between the native handicraft workers and the buyers. There is no assistance from the department and there has been a reliance on the Hudson's Bay Company for any trade that is done.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the vote carry?
I thought the minister was on the verge of giving some answer on the points raised by the hon. member for Timis-kaming, and I want to make some comments myself.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
With reference to the case raised by the hon. member, if he cares to give the name of the person involved I shall undertake to have the case looked into. But

so far as the general activity is concerned this vote is to authorize moneys to provide, in respect of Indian commercial activities, for the instruction and supervision of Indians, the furnishing of materials, the purchase of finished goods and the sale of such finished goods. Is there organized assistance for Indians in the handicraft field in the same way as there is for Eskimos under northern affairs? The Eskimos have been assisted in forming co-operatives so they can do this work. I am interested in the Ontario Indians, particularly the Manitoulin Indians and the Temagami Indians, bands of the type that have been operating as tightly knit organizations. Does the department send in people to train them and give advice as to what kind of products can be sold? The little bird or animal that the Eskimos have has been a pretty good deal for them and I wonder whether similar assistance has been given to the Indians.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know how closely the two programs can be compared, the one for the Eskimos and the one for the Indians. However, there is this development program for the Indians which provides assistance for their training in handicrafts and in selling their products. As I said a moment ago, it will be noted from this particular vote that the project seems to have gone particularly well and there seems to be a sharply increased demand for this kind of developmental assistance. That is the reason we are in these supplementaries asking for an amount greater than the amount in the main estimates under this heading.

Is there any way that the department can protect the Indians against the importation of facsimiles? I refer to totem poles, Indian type slippers and Indian type beaded belts. We find them being imported from Japan. When you buy them at an outfitter's shop you find they are stamped "made in Japan". Because this is a protected field and because the Indians are having such a difficult job adjusting to our business community, I am wondering whether we have considered the idea of restricting the sale of facsimiles in Canada.

speechtext:
The hon. member has raised a pretty large question. As he knows, any
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration imports into this country require to have the country of origin marked on them. Then there is the protection to be obtained, as was the case with Ookpik, through the trade mark legislation or design mark legislation, or possibly the copyright legislation. In certain circumstances these acts can all be applicable to certain products. About all I can do now is to draw the minister's attention to this point to make sure that the department is applying the existing legislation to the maximum extent possible to protect the products of the Indians in the handicraft field.

Mr. Chairman, with regard to what the minister has just said, unfortunately the native Indian people do not know anything about copyrights or copyrighting for design and that sort of thing. Although it may be a bit late now, it might be a worthwhile venture for them to try to establish their rights, especially the west coast Indians who developed totemic carving. Incidentally, this carving is the only truly original North American art form developed on this continent. These carvings appear on totems, house poles, house fronts and now on plaques. These figures represent the inheritance of families of Indian people and are truly theirs if anything is theirs. Other countries have seized upon them and they now come back to this country in the form, for instance, of grotesque totems from Japan. They are sold as authentic Indian totemic carvings when in fact they are not.
A prime example of this is in the field of the argillite carving of the Haida Indians of the Queen Charlotte islands. For many years they have carved their tribal stories, their crests and the like on a slate called argillite and the work they do is beautiful. Many of the younger fellows are now taking up the old art handed down to them from their forefathers. These carvings are representative of an art and culture far surpassing most other art forms that exist in North America today. They bring a reasonably decent price. The price for an argillite totem carving is anywhere from $6 to $7 an inch and if they are larger poles, say three feet high, the price can range up to $20 or $25 an inch and in some cases more than that. They are well worth it too because of the beauty of the work that is done.
However, right in north Vancouver, British Columbia, there is a company operated by an individual by the name of Boris Mange who bought or somehow acquired some of the original authentic argillite carvings depicting the stories of two or three Haida families. I do not know exactly what his process is, but

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration it is a chemical process involving the breaking down or liquefying of fibreglass which is then poured into rubber moulds and out of the mould comes a flat object which is scratch by scratch the same as the original. From a distance of a foot or two one cannot tell the difference between an artificial totem and an original carving. It is only when one picks up the artificial carving, holds it in his hand, finds it is much lighter and looks on the bottom that he finds it is not an authentic carving at all. It is only by close examination that this can be discerned.
These mouldings or castings have been sold and are probably still being sold in shops all across Canada. They are represented as authentic Haida or Indian carvings. I saw them first a year and a half or two years ago in a jeweller's shop on Elgin street. I was walking by the shop and saw this carving in the store. I was amazed to see them in Ottawa and I went inside to inquire about them. I had a lengthy argument with the operator of the shop as to their authenticity. He showed me a communication from a wholesaler in Toronto-I have forgotten the name -to the effect that these were authentic argillite carvings.
They were not authentic at all, they were substitutes. I have seen similar signs in other curio shops in different parts of Canada representing these mouldings or castings as authentic Haida argillite carvings. They are not. All that is shown on them is a shortened version of the individual's name on the bottom. This could be interpreted by those not familiar with the peculiarities of one of our native tongues on the west coast as the name of the individual. In fact, it is not. It is a shortened version of the name Boris Mange.
How does one protect himself against the mechanism of the individual whose sole concern is not the production of anything artistic or cultural but the production of a commodity purely for profit? Our native Indian people are not conversant with the copyright law. In fact, I understand from people in the legal field that this is a specialized branch of law which is highly complex. One almost has to make a lifetime study of the Copyright Act in order to appreciate all the intricacies of it. I believe that the crown, some government agency, could make a particular study of the copyright law and assist the native Indian people in attempting to protect, by law, their own designs which represent their inheritance from their families.
Whether or not this has ever been suggested before, I could not say. It was only upon invitation, following the minister's explanation, that I rose to deal with the question. I would appreciate some answer from the Minister of Justice or perhaps the Minister of Transport


who at one time was the minister of citizenship and immigration. Could a study be made of the copyright law to see whether or not it could be used to assist the native Indian people to protect their own designs, and particularly the designs of the west coast people in their totemic art?

That is the history of opportunity for bilingual civil servants in Ottawa. That is why I am so very pleased with the work now being done by the government, part of it through this estimate, in making available training facilities to enable present civil servants to become bilingual more readily. This is a need in our country that is very real; and it is a mistake to say that there has been any discrimination against or any frustration on the part of any section of the civil service on account of language. That simply is not so, and has not been the case.

I should like to make a comment on this interesting and important point which has been raised. I believe the government should consider the creation of a new category within the civil service for those who are truly bilingual. I do not place

in this category a person like myself; although I can understand and read French, I cannot express myself in the French language in the way I should like. The reason for this is simple; it is because I am thinking in English, and to be able to think in English and express myself with precision in French I would require training similar to that of the simultaneous interpreters we have in the chamber.
We have examples of what I mean in the civil service, and good examples here in the house. Some hon. members have not one person living in their constituencies who speak French. Other hon. members may not have one person living in their constituencies who speaks the English language. I think that if an hon. member of this type has a bilingual secretary, what happens after three or four years is that his bilingual secretary becomes a unilingual secretary. If you do not practise both languages constantly, sooner or later one of them is lost. I recall hearing a former member say that it is not enough to have a language in your head; you must also have it on your tongue before you become fluent.
Let me take as an example the riding of Danforth in Toronto. I do not think there is any need for the hon. member for Danforth to have a bilingual secretary. Similarly I do not think there is any need for the hon. member for Beauce to have a bilingual secretary. But for members from a constituency like mine, which is half French speaking and half English speaking, and in many other constituencies across the country similarly divided, I think there is a very definite need for a bilingual secretary. Many times I have difficulty and am put to delay and considerable personal expense in getting my letters translated so that I can reply to my constituents in the language with which they are more familiar. I can read their letters but I cannot write back without my words being correctly translated. If you do not know a language well and try to write it, it is easy to make a tragic mistake which can backfire badly.
I recall going to the United States not many years ago, and when I was near Boston, Massachusetts, I had occasion to go to a garage, the proprietor of which had a French name. I talked to him and found that he came not too far from where I was born and raised in the province of Quebec. He came from Magog, which is about the same distance from Sherbrooke as my town, but on the other side. I spoke to him in French and to my surprise he said he was sorry, that he did not speak French. He told me he had been there for eight years, it is unbelievable that a man can forget his mother

tongue in eight years. But that was true, and was because he never had the chance to speak French.
I think that where there is a need for a truly bilingual person in the civil service a special category should be created and a rate of pay offered as an encouragement. It is not the easiest thing in the world, particularly for a person from the far reaches of Canada, to prepare to handle a job of this kind. However, I think this is something which is needed, and needed badly, and people who have this facility are a great deal more valuable than those who have only the one language or the other. Therefore I think the government should consider the creation of a special category and provide a special rate of pay for people with this ability.

I should like to ask the minister who is handling these estimates a question concerning the operations of the civil service commission having to do with the manner in which it establishes so-called eligibility lists for vacant positions. I do not know if I am using the right term, but apparently if a vacancy is posted people can bid on that particular job and then take an examination of some sort. Following the examination a list is established of the people eligible for that particular position. What policy is there with regard to the length of time that such an eligibility list is valid after it is originally established?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Appointments, as the hon. member knows, are made from the top of the list when the list is established. Normally the list is retained for one year. The period of time for which a list remains valid is determined by the commission itself but my understanding is that normally it is a year, although in the case of a large class where there is a very long list and few have been called the commission may maintain the list for a longer period, and sometimes does.

I wish to object to the procedure of establishing closed eligibility lists even for a period of a year, and I would certainly object even more strongly to establishing them for a longer period of time. I am aware of an instance or two in this field and it was because of them that this matter first came to my attention.
Presumably the process of opening up a vacancy to competition is to give people who feel they are qualified the opportunity to bid for the job, and the person who establishes qualifications greater than those of the other contestants is posted to the position. But when you maintain a list of this sort in existence for a period of one year you are then preventing, should a vacancy occur in the same position, anybody else from bidding for the particular job, because a list has been established and that is it. It is closed and it is valid for a particular period of time.
In some cases this works to the detriment of individuals. I know of a case in point about which I have had correspondence with the commission. The circumstances were that a position became vacant and was filled. Then the job subsequently became vacant again within a very short period of time because the person who originally filled it was promoted to a higher position. A woman working in the same section of the department, who knew the office procedure, the personnel, the

Supply-Secretary of State problems and so on, asked for the right to bid on the particular job and was advised she could not because there was a closed list in effect. The next eligible person on that list lived in a community some 500 miles away by air and 900 miles away by road, and the woman who wanted to bid on the job was told she would have to wait to see whether this woman who was some 900 miles away by road was going to take it.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has just complained to me, Mr. Chairman, that I am speaking so loudly he cannot hear the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm.
This woman found herself prevented from even bidding for the vacant position, because of this closed list. I think this is unduly restrictive and interferes with what I consider to be the normal and reasonable right of a person, under the civil service structure, to bid for a job and to take a test to see whether or not he or she can fill the particular position.
Perhaps the maintenance of an eligibility list for a period of a month would not be an unreasonable interference with a person's right to bid for a new job, because I can see that all sorts of difficulties might arise when a person takes a new position. Although he has passed the test and qualifies for the position some difficulty may develop, with the result that he cannot fill the position or, as was the case in this instance, he may be promoted to a higher position. There are a variety of difficulties which might crop up and could result in the person's being found unsuitable or leaving the job within a period of a month, and it might result in unnecessary expense if the whole process of conducting a competition had to be gone through again.
But a one year period is far too long a time to maintain an eligibility list. 1 think people in the public service would be treated much more fairly if the minister, or somebody else, would take steps to see that the length of time eligibility lists are maintained is considerably shortened. In this way the right of the individual employee, according to what I understand is a principle of the operations of the civil service commission, to bid for a vacant, more senior and higher paid position and to enter into a competition with others for the particular job would be preserved. Once you have a list established you interfere with this principle for at least that period of time.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that this large and rather important aspect of the hiring practices of the civil service commission is one that should be debated when the minister to whom the commission is answerable is presenting his main estimates.


Rather than attempting to argue the matter now I would prefer to leave it for debate and discussion at that time. However, I will see that the point raised by the hon. member is drawn to the attention of the minister specifically concerned.

I have communicated these views to the commission in a much shorter form, because they are contained in a letter and I wanted to express them publicly. I did not really expect to enter into conversation with anyone as to the propriety of my suggestion. I simply wished to air the matter publicly so that it would be on the record. The minister has indicated that cognizance will be taken of the point and I hope that some alteration will be made as a result.

Mr. Chairman, everybody
knows that French speaking employees earning $5,000 or more a year, in all the federal departments, represent about 5 per cent of the total.
When the Minister of Justice made his statement in Toronto, the civil service association raised protests. If the Minister of Justice made such a statement, it was certainly justified.
It is for that reason that I am asking the government what they intend to do to correct or improve this situation. We all know that during the last election campaign, the Secretary of State and others travelled throughout the province of Quebec stating that the French speaking civil servants were discriminated against and did not have a fair share of positions. Well then, I am wondering what the government intends to do to remedy this situation.
As I said before, the government has spent hundreds of dollars to create the royal commission on biculturalism in order to try and find a solution to the problem, but in practice, the present government refuses to face up to its responsibilities and to take positive action.
Let me give an example, if I may. During the last session, the Minister of Industry appointed two deputy ministers, neither one was French speaking. I ask the minister once again whether he intends to carry out the suggestions made by the Secretary of State during the last election campaign, in view of the fact that those undertakings were published in all French newspapers. Does the minister intend to give a bonus or a special pay rate to bilingual Canadians, whether they be French or English speaking? I should like to have a specific answer from the minister; otherwise, we would have to force the government to state its position, even if we have to discuss this item for three weeks.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No. I would like to know from the Minister of Justice, who is responsible for the fair treatment of all Canadian citizens and who has the great responsibility of administering justice in the country, whether he intends to implement the promises made by the Secretary of State to the effect that bilingual Canadians-of either French or English origin-employed by the federal government should get an increased salary when they speak two languages and possess two cultures.
Is the item carried?

No, Mr. Chairman. I would like to say this: I know that most members on the government side do not agree with the views expressed by the Secretary of State and do not want by any means that the French culture should spread in the civil service and that bilingual Canadians should take their rightful place within the civil service, whether they are French or English speaking.
But what I cannot understand is that, during the last election, the Secretary of State made promises throughout Quebec, saying that if the Liberals came into power, bilingual Canadians would get a fair treatment and benefit from a special bonus for being able to speak both languages.
It is all very fine to have a royal commission on bilingualism and to try rousing Canadian opinion from sea to sea, but I think that it is high time for the government to go ahead and take some action. The government should tell us what it intends to do, whether it means to keep the promises made by the Secretary of State and grant a special bonus to bilingual employees in the federal civil service to those in the higher positions.
That is what we want to know. Even if the members sitting on the treasury benches try to have this item rushed through, I want to obtain a precise answer, I want the responsible minister to simply tell us: we shall grant a special bonus to bilingual employees or we shall not.
